abstract: Humans and other animals have strictly limited working memory capacity. When asked to recall one or more presented items after a delay period, subjects will occasionally recall an apparently random item: a "guess'' response. Where do these guesses come from? Using electrophysiological recordings from across monkey neocortex during the performance of a color working memory task, we show that the neural correlates of guess responses emerge during the memory delay -- and that variable encoding precision makes guesses more likely, especially in one of our two animals. If guess responses emerge due to noise, we hypothesize that the detailed neural population geometry for color should shape the distribution of behavioral responses. We confirm this hypothesis by showing that the representational geometry specific to each animal is consistent with their idiosyncratic patterns of errors. Despite the often assumed robustness of neural population representations, noise appears to be a key bottleneck on the reliability of working memory.
